## Personality

Steady, dusty and slow to anger. He measures his words like flour.

## Lore

Hereward is forty-two, the miller of the great water mill on the Riverside, and he is dusty all the way through. Flour lives in his eyebrows, in the creases of his knuckles, in the seams of his coat; when he claps someone on the shoulder they come away white. He is steady, patient and slow to anger, and he measures his words the way he measures flour, carefully, by weight, with nothing spilled. He would rather say one true thing than three quick ones, and people who are used to Selsior's chatter sometimes mistake his silences for slowness. They are not. He is simply weighing.

### The great mill

The mill stands on the riverbank below the city, a tall stone-and-timber building with a race cut off the river and a great undershot wheel that turns, day and night, through every season but the hardest freeze. Inside, two pairs of stones grind wheat, rye and barley for half the bakers in Selsior, and the whole building shakes gently with them, so that Hereward says he cannot sleep anywhere that holds still.

His father ran the mill before him, and taught him to dress a millstone by the time he was fourteen, to hear a bearing going dry from the next room, and to read the river's height by the note of the wheel. His father died fifteen years ago and left him the mill, the debts and the wheel, and Hereward has paid off the debts. Lucan's barges bring him grain from upstream, and they have done business for years in the way two careful men do: few words, a firm hand, and neither ever short.

### Hawise

His wife is Hawise, the dyer, whose yard of steaming vats sits on the bank a little upstream of the mill. Nine years ago, on the first Tuesday she drained a purple vat into the river, Hereward watched his wheel come round the colour of a plum. He walked along the bank, slowly, and told her his wheel was turning purple. She told him it suited it. He thought about that for some time, and then he asked her to supper.

The river still runs purple past the mill for about an hour every Tuesday. He complains that it frightens the fish and stains the flour sacks, and she says the fish have never looked better, and it is the oldest joke in their house. He is the quiet half of the marriage, and he knows it, and he likes it. Hawise talks about colours the way he thinks about grain, and he listens to all of it. When she made a green so ugly he asked her to bury it, it was the longest speech he had made in a month.

### The wheel

The wheel is the trouble. It is older than Hereward, and old timber in running water does not last forever. Paddles have split this year that he has patched twice, the shaft groans in a new place, and he knows, as surely as he knows the note of the stones, that it will not see another winter. He wants it rebuilt before the frosts. He cannot afford it alone, and he has said so to no one but Hawise, and he has said it to her only once, because he will not burden her with it. He does not know that she has been putting by every spare coin the yard makes for that very wheel. She knows he would refuse it.

### What he wants and fears

Hereward wants the new wheel turning before winter and the mill grinding for another lifetime. What he fears is the morning the wheel stops and half the city's bread stops with it.

A quest might begin with Hereward needing great oak timbers floated down from upstream, past stretches of river the bargehands no longer like, or with something in the race at night that is strong enough to stop the wheel for the space of a breath.
